chapter: Sanger, Ben Black and carnival balls
title: Keeping peace at dances, bouncer Chuck Connors and the World Series
summary: He tells of buying a beer to defuse an angry patron, prize-fighter floor managers in New York and a World Series game.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: I said, we all that shit.

We were friends. I remember when I was in one of those country towns, we just played the carnival ball and had the tabloid, we were tied a little bit, and it was my custom, after the carnival ball, to play one set and take another mission. So the band's on and I'm straightening up things. And some country hit comes up to me, where's the music, where's the music, where's the music, what do you mean? I paid to come in here. I said, I know you're paid to come in here. I said, we just got through playing the ball. I said, get the drink. I said, I'm going to get a beer. Will you have one? I bought him a beer and it was my friend for life. Just to show you, you've got to use diplomacy. I got sassy with that guy, I wouldn't have been able to blow the rest of the night, he popped me right in the mouth. But I said, I'm going to get the beer, come on, come with me. We go down and drink a couple of beers. He was my bodyguard all night. Up in the Balkan A's where I played, we had two prize fighters, floor managers, you know, they wore tuxedos. One was Chuck Connors, an ex-heavyweight prize fighter. And I was there, that year the World Series was in New York, and he says to me, you want to go to the World Series? I get you. And I was asking me. I said, sure. I said, meet him. I meet him at the Polar Grounds. He said, I can't find a guy. That wasn't that. He wanted me to take him into the boat. You know, into the boat. So I said, well that's all right, forget about it. I got the dough. I gave the guy ten bucks. It was three dollars a piece. He don't give any change. I said to the guy, is it ten dollars, five dollars a ticket? He said, no, it's three. I said, well, it's a change. Oh, I forgot. I said, if you average four dollars out of every ten dollars that comes into this window, you're going to have a good day, mister. New York is the most famous short change place in the world. People rush for the subway, give them all that change. Not me, I'm not giving a guy ten dollars when I know two tickets, only six dollars. And I saw the World Series, but the next day I didn't go take Chuck Connors, he didn't go find another sucker. And in fact a guy told me, weren't you at the polo grounds? I said, yeah, got a bad record. Pick him up, they might pick you up. But he was a bouncer in my time. Oh, I had a lot of experience. I had Jack Stone, the Australian middleweight, he gave me his picture and he said, although you are far from home, you can always depend on Jack Stone. And if he saw everybody get rambunctious near the bandstand, he'd come sidling up there and break it up.
Who was playing the World Series then? Do you remember?

Washington was one of the teams because the New Orleans boy Joe Martino pitched one in in while the great Matthews had somebody warmed up. Yeah that's why I was so interested in it because we had New Orleans pitchers to them. Sixty-five thousand people looking at the ball game. When that ball game was over I never saw so many people rush for the streetcars and what was a big shot and looked for a taxi cab. And I was just as hard to get into the streetcar. Taxi cab was about twenty cents a mile or something. Everything was cheap. I had wonderful experiences. Ask me something that's of interest to you though.
